Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}\frac{xy-y}{x-1}=\frac{1\cdot (-3)-(-3)}{1-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}\frac{xy-y}{x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}\frac{(x-1)y}{x-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-3.$

questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{1+2}}{3-1-2}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2}}{x-y-2} & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y+2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}-(\sqrt{y+2})^{2}}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{x-y-2}{(x-y-2)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (3,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y+2}} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{1+2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y}=\frac{{1}^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{({y}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{(\sqrt{x}-y)(\sqrt{x}+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{({y}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{-(x-{y}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+y)}{x-{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y) & =-(\sqrt{1}+1) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+x+y}{xy+{y}^{2}}=\frac{(-1)^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1+(-1)+1}{(-1)\cdot 1+{1}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+x+y}{xy+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x(x+y)+(x+y)}{y(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{(x+1)(x+y)}{y(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y} & =\frac{(-1)+1}{1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $0.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$
